title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as Savings
dek: The housing provident fund is not a savings account you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take, you should still take.
why: Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, and a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the system-inside track is especially informative.
who: Employees with a housing fund who aren't sure whether to withdraw or leave it; people considering buying a home, converting a commercial loan to a provident-fund loan, or contributing as flexible-employment workers; job seekers trying to judge whether a company is well-run.
skip: The opening chit-chat about how the episode came about and the three hosts' positions can be fast-forwarded; start at 13:10 with Zhou Yi's account of actually using it.

points.h: Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
points.body: After Zhou Yi set up Beijing's no-threshold monthly rent withdrawal of 2,000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; by month's end, once her spending card was maxed out, it was auto-deducted, adding friction to daily life. After confirming the fund balance earns 1.5% interest, higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit, she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yu Bai noted this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you can, use everything you can’, and two young colleagues in the department had made the same choice. Lao Qian cautioned that this is indeed low capital efficiency, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine — people just make fake books for themselves.

points.h: The housing fund is not a deposit; not being able to withdraw is the norm
points.body: Yu Bai walked through an extreme scenario: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands in the housing fund, but the home is self-occupied, so it qualifies neither for buying nor renting; even if the new rules allow withdrawal for renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs, they're stuck. If they risk fraudulent withdrawal under a fabricated pretext, they must return the full amount and are barred from any withdrawal for three years. So both ‘take everything you can’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a higher rate than a current account’ are valid — it depends on the individual.

points.h: The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order
points.body: This revision adjusts 20 clauses. First, renovating a self-occupied home and paying its property fees are included as withdrawal purposes for the first time; the fund no longer serves only mortgage buying. Second, renting used to require rent exceeding a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that limit and puts renting first in the withdrawal order. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally included in the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers can contribute voluntarily and apply for provident-fund loans. In addition, the management center must reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being advanced.

points.h: The share of contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
points.body: Lao Qian's data: this year, the share of housing-fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, versus over 70% at the peak — a steady decline in just a few years. That is, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality loan channel is actually used by only just over 30% of people. This directly reflects how low the desire to buy is. Lao Qian also points out the new rules aim at housing consumption, not leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation can be withdrawn, thresholds greatly lowered — supporting measures as the real-estate market shifts from incremental to stock, and also echoing aging: the monthly withdrawal ratio turned up in 2023, exactly when the 1960s cohort retired.

points.h: If you want to buy, be careful about withdrawing your fund
points.body: Yu Bai warns: provident-fund loan limits are tied to account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou has multiple caps; when applying, the smallest of several standards applies, e.g., for a first or second self-occupied home the minimum down payment is 20%, so a 1 million yuan home can't be loaned more than 800,000; also, monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income is not allowed. So before withdrawing the fund as living expenses, check your city's loan rules. Yu Bai is also cautious about the buy logic of ‘rent-to-price ratio near the provident-fund rate, only a down payment short’: you must also consider depreciation, price swings, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 down payment is locked up.

points.h: Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
points.body: For flexible-employment workers, the contribution base and rate are calculated the same as for employees, but there's no employer paying half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed; above 10,000 you must log into the tax app and check your tax details as documentation, to prevent over-declaring to extract a higher loan limit. Zhou Yi did the math: 10,000 at 10% to 24% is 1,000 to 2,400 yuan, and this money is not counted in personal income tax, but if unused it's a loss. Also, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before applying for a provident-fund loan, and most do not allow one-time back payments.

points.h: Inside the system, the housing fund is an invisible benefit
points.body: Zhou Yi asked a friend with a public-institution job back home, who openly showed a screenshot of their fund account: monthly deposits were more than double hers, and the balance already exceeded her savings; the friend lives at home with no rent need, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus a职业年金 on top, and the contribution base includes all bonuses and subsidies. Lao Qian adds: the fund is tax-free, and with personal pensions capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal, those inside the system get an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the national average annual wage for urban non-private units was 129,441 yuan, for private units 71,590 yuan — while working hours run the other way.

points.h: Full housing-fund contributions are a slice for judging a company
points.body: Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the housing fund a more ideal choice’ hasn't changed at all: a company that pays the full housing fund respects its employees and respects the rules, meaning it's likely well-run in every aspect, not playing cat-and-mouse with policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximization the first goal, treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi calculated: a wage base of 100, take-home just over 70, but the boss pays over 130 — everyone in the chain feels wronged. Lao Qian cites Ford's Model T wage increase — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it wasn't capitalist conscience, it was a better utility function.

quotes.text: It arrived, but because your phone gets so many app notifications, you don't look carefully — say it reminds you 2,000 yuan came in, and it just sits in that card until the end of the month, when my spending card is maxed out and it gets auto-deducted from that card.
But the fact is people make fake books for themselves, people withdraw on impulse for all sorts of reasons, people are very good at self-deception.
You really can't treat the housing fund as a deposit, because your bank deposit you can withdraw anytime, but the housing fund you can't.
And it's the highest-quality loan channel, the rate is so low, yet only just over 30% of people took a loan — at the peak it was over 70% — in just a few years.
I think a company that pays the full housing fund shows it respects its employees and respects the rules.

Treating people as people doesn't mean increasing costs; it also means one person's spending — the household sector's spending — becomes the corporate sector's income, and the corporate sector's spending becomes the household sector's wages. These two form a virtuous cycle.
Take everything you can, use everything you can — buying a home, building, renovating, repaying a loan, renting, retirement, leaving the country — all can use it.
